en: To accept or agree to something reluctantly but without protest
hook: ACQUIESCE: 'ACQUI-YES', saying a quiet yes.
story: Nadia wanted to celebrate her birthday at a restaurant, but her parents insisted on a family dinner at home. After a long sigh, she acquiesced. She wasn't happy, but she didn't argue. To acquiesce is to accept something quietly, often reluctantly.

en: Clever or skillful in using the hands or mind
hook: ADROIT: 'a-DROIT' (French for right-handed), skillful.
story: The adroit negotiator turned a heated argument into a deal in twenty minutes, calming both sides and finding common ground. Adroit means skillful and clever, especially in handling difficult situations. It's a synonym of deft and dexterous.

en: To make changes in order to improve or correct
hook: AMEND: MEND something to make it better.
story: After protests, parliament amended the law to protect students' rights. Rafi also amended his essay after his teacher's feedback, fixing errors and adding examples. To amend is to change for the better. To make amends means to repair the harm you've done.

en: Hostility or strong dislike
hook: ANIMUS: like an ANIMAL's growl toward an enemy.
story: The animus between the two rival coaching centers was obvious: they tore down each other's posters and spread rumors about each other's teachers. Animus means strong hostility or ill-will. Synonyms: animosity, antipathy, enmity.

en: A person who defends a controversial idea, person, or cause
hook: GRE trick: an APOLOGIST doesn't apologize — he DEFENDS.
story: Even after the dictator's crimes were exposed, a few apologists still defended him on TV, insisting he had done good for the nation. An apologist is a person who argues in defense of something controversial. It has nothing to do with saying sorry; that's a classic GRE trap.

en: Sharply severe or critical; also, causing skin tissue to contract
hook: ASTRINGENT: like a STRINGENT, tight squeeze, harsh.
story: The editor's astringent comments filled the margins of Arif's manuscript: 'Weak.' 'Lazy.' 'Rewrite.' No softening at all. Astringent means sharply severe in manner or criticism. Astringent lotions tighten skin pores; astringent words tighten your stomach.

en: To work jointly with others; to cooperate with an enemy
bn: সহযোগিতা করা; শত্রুর সাথে আঁতাত করা
hook: CO-LABOR-ATE: LABOR together.
story: Mitu and Sara collaborated on their research paper: one handled the data, the other the writing. Together, they won first prize. To collaborate is to work together. Historically, it can also mean cooperating traitorously with an enemy, as collaborators did during wartime.

en: Having enough skill or knowledge to do something successfully
hook: COMPETENT: able to COMPETE.
story: Tanvir isn't the best programmer in the office, but he's competent; every task he takes on gets done correctly and on time. Competent means having the necessary ability. A competent doctor may not be famous, but you can trust her.

en: To have a mutual relationship in which one thing affects or depends on another
hook: CO-RELATE: RELATED together.
story: Researchers found that hours of sleep correlated with GRE scores: students who slept more scored higher. But correlation isn't causation; maybe good students just organize their time better. To correlate is to show a connection between two things. GRE arguments love this trap.

en: To mock or express contempt for
hook: DE-RIDE: laughing (ride, from Latin 'ridere') DOWN at someone.
story: When Rafi first said he wanted to become a professional chess player, his relatives derided him: 'Chess? Is that even a job?' Ten years later, he became a grandmaster. To deride is to ridicule and mock. Many great ideas were derided before they succeeded.

en: To give orders with authority; to control or determine
hook: DICTATE: what a DICTATOR does.
story: Nadia's busy schedule dictated that she study only from five to seven each morning; there was no other free time. Her boss also liked to dictate every detail of her work. To dictate is to command or to determine. Common sense dictates that you shouldn't drive tired.

en: Careful in what one says or does, to avoid causing offense or revealing secrets
hook: DISCREET keeps secrets; DISCRETE means separate. Two E's together are 'discreet' — they keep each other's secrets.
story: When Arif told his colleague about his job interview with another company, she was discreet and never mentioned it to anyone. Discreet means careful and tactful, able to keep private matters private. Don't confuse it with discrete, which means separate and distinct.

en: Separated or disconnected from something
hook: GRE trick: DIVORCED FROM reality means disconnected from it.
story: The minister's speech about everyone's rising prosperity seemed completely divorced from reality; outside, people were standing in line for cheap rice. On the GRE, divorced from means separated from or unconnected to something. A theory divorced from evidence is just a guess.

en: Believing that a select group is superior and deserves special treatment
hook: ELITIST: thinks only the ELITE matter.
story: The club only admitted members from three expensive schools and looked down on everyone else. Critics called it elitist. Elitist means believing a small, privileged group is superior. An elitist attitude toward education says only the rich deserve the best schools.

en: Making great demands on skill, attention, or effort
bn: কঠোর পরিশ্রম দাবি করে এমন; অতি খুঁতখুঁতে
hook: EXACTING: demands everything to be EXACT.
story: The violin teacher was exacting: every note had to be perfect, every finger placed precisely. One tiny error meant playing the whole piece again. Exacting means very demanding, requiring precision and effort. An exacting task stretches you to your limit.

en: Bewildered; completely confused
hook: FLUMMOXED: sounds like your brain just got FLUMMOXED, flopped and mixed.
story: The first GRE quant question was so strange that Tanvir sat flummoxed for two minutes, staring at it without knowing where to begin. Flummoxed means utterly confused and perplexed. It's a fun synonym for befuddled and baffled.

en: Producing good or helpful results; productive
hook: FRUITFUL: a tree full of FRUIT.
story: The two-hour meeting was surprisingly fruitful: they solved three problems, agreed on a budget, and planned the launch. Fruitful means productive, giving good results. A fruitful discussion leads somewhere; a fruitless one wastes time.

en: Existing from birth; natural
hook: IN-BORN: BORN INside you.
story: Sara's younger brother had an inborn talent for music; at four, he could play any song on the harmonium after hearing it once. Nobody taught him. Inborn means natural, existing from birth. It's a synonym of innate.

en: A person with expert knowledge in many subjects
hook: POLY = many, MATH = learning. Learned in many things.
story: Leonardo da Vinci was the ultimate polymath: painter, engineer, anatomist, inventor, and musician. Rabindranath Tagore was a polymath too: poet, painter, composer, and educator. A polymath has deep knowledge across many fields.

en: Not revealing one's thoughts or feelings readily
hook: RETICENT: keeps words RETAINED, held back.
story: When asked about his time in prison, the old freedom fighter was reticent. He changed the subject, smiled quietly, and said only, 'It was hard.' Reticent means reserved, unwilling to share feelings. Note: reticent isn't the same as reluctant, though people often confuse them.

en: Strict, precise, and exacting
hook: STRINGENT: tied up with tight STRINGS.
story: The university had stringent admission requirements: a GRE score of 325, three recommendation letters, and an interview. Only five percent of applicants got in. Stringent means very strict. Stringent safety rules protect factory workers.

en: Prepared to obey others without question; excessively submissive
hook: SUB-SERVIENT: a SERVANT, below (sub) everyone.
story: The assistant was so subservient that he agreed with every word his boss said, even when the boss contradicted himself in the same sentence. Subservient means overly obedient and submissive. Synonyms: servile, obsequious.

en: Kept secret, especially because it would not be approved of
hook: SURREPTITIOUS: SURE-REPTILE-ish, sneaking like a lizard.
story: During the boring lecture, Rafi took surreptitious bites of his sandwich, hiding it behind his notebook whenever the professor turned around. Surreptitious means done secretly and stealthily. It's a synonym of furtive and clandestine.

en: Tempting, but out of reach
hook: TANTALIZING: from TANTALUS, punished with fruit and water just out of reach forever.
story: The smell of biryani drifted from the kitchen during Ramadan, tantalizing everyone two hours before iftar. In Greek myth, Tantalus stood in water that drained away whenever he tried to drink. Tantalizing means teasingly tempting, especially when you can't have it yet.

en: Equivalent in seriousness or effect to
hook: TANTAMOUNT: amounts to the same AMOUNT.
story: Staying silent while your friend cheats on the exam is tantamount to helping him cheat. The effect is the same. Tantamount means equivalent to, usually used for something bad. Refusing to answer the question was tantamount to admitting guilt.

en: A state of physical or mental inactivity; lethargy
hook: TORPOR: like a TORPEDO that never launched, just sits there.
story: After the heavy Eid lunch, the whole family sank into torpor, sprawled on sofas, too sluggish even to talk. Some animals enter torpor in winter to save energy. Torpor is a state of inactivity and sluggishness. Synonyms: lethargy, inertia.

en: Vigorously effective and sharply clear in expression
hook: TRENCHANT: cuts like a sharp blade digging a TRENCH.
story: In just three sentences, the journalist's trenchant analysis exposed the flaws in the government's policy. Readers said it cut straight to the heart of the issue. Trenchant means incisive and sharply clear. A trenchant critic doesn't waste words.

en: Offense or annoyance
hook: UMBRAGE: you take UMBRAGE and go sit in the shade (umbra) to sulk.
story: When Nadia joked that her uncle's cooking was 'interesting,' he took umbrage and didn't speak to her for the rest of dinner. To take umbrage is to feel offended. The word comes from 'umbra', or shadow: a dark cloud of resentment.

en: Able to adapt to many different functions or activities
hook: VERSATILE: works in every VERSE, every situation.
story: Arif is a versatile cricketer: he bowls spin, opens the batting, and keeps wicket when needed. A versatile tool, like a Swiss Army knife, serves many purposes. Versatile means adaptable, with many skills or uses.

en: Difficult to control because of unpredictable or disobedient behavior
hook: WAYWARD: going AWAY from the right path.
story: The wayward teenager skipped school, stayed out late, and ignored every rule his parents set. His grandmother kept praying he'd return to the right path. Wayward means unruly and disobedient. A wayward kite drifts in random directions in the wind.
